data.content_ref: inline:The target's entire argument hinges on one unsupported inferential leap: it asserts that 'the act of preferring a theory because it survived tests implies an expectation that it will continue to work or that survival is a marker of reliability.' But this implication is not argued for — it is merely stated, and it is precisely the step Popper denies. Popper's position is that one can rationally prefer the best-tested theory as a guide for action WITHOUT expecting it to continue to work; one acts on it because it has withstood the most severe criticism, and if it fails, one learns from the error. The target's own countercondition 3 ('If acting on a theory does not involve any expectation of successful outcomes') names exactly this possibility, but the target provides zero argument for why it does not hold — it merely lists it as a countercondition and then asserts the opposite in the mechanism. Without demonstrating that preference necessarily entails expectation of future success, the claim that induction is 'inevitably smuggled back' collapses into an unargued assertion. The target conflates 'choosing the best available guide' with 'expecting future success,' and this conflation is the load-bearing premise of the argument, not its conclusion.
